after: ## What each area of law typically covers
alt: Three columns. Employment law (contracts, minimum wage, hours, holiday, fair treatment and dismissal) protects employees. Health and safety law (risk assessment, safe equipment, training, protective clothing, accident reporting) protects employees and visitors. Consumer law (goods as described, safe products, accurate labels, honest adverts, refunds) protects customers.
caption: Each area of law sets minimum standards that protect a different group.

after: ## Assessing the impact: the four headings in the specification
alt: A business law at the centre with four impacts: cost (wages, equipment, inspections, insurance), training needs (safe methods, fair recruitment, refund rights), recruitment (non-discriminatory adverts, contracts, right-to-work checks) and the consequences of failing to comply (fines, compensation, closure orders, recalls, prosecution, bad publicity).
caption: Explain a law’s effect through cost, training, recruitment or the penalties for breaking it.

after: ## Assessing the impact: the four headings in the specification
alt: Legal consequences of breaking business law: fines, compensation, orders to stop using unsafe equipment or close premises, product recalls and, in serious cases, prosecution of managers. Bad publicity follows, losing the trust of customers and future employees, and often costs more than the fine.
caption: Penalties hurt, and lost trust can cost more than any fine.

after: ## National minimum wage: benefits and drawbacks
alt: Juniper Cafés pays 20 staff for 35,000 hours a year (20 × 35 × 50). A 60-cent rise from $7.20 to $7.80 adds $21,000 a year, which is $0.14 on each of 150,000 meals. Juniper can raise prices, accept lower profit or use fewer hours.
caption: A 60-cent wage rise costs Juniper $21,000 a year, or 14 cents a meal.

alt: Three requirements and their effects: safe products that work as described mean more spending on design, testing and quality control; accurate packaging and adverts mean checking marketing claims; and repairs, replacements or refunds for faulty goods mean returns procedures and trained staff.
caption: Consumer law shapes what a business sells and how it sells it.

alt: Brackwell must recall 2,000 faulty kettles; 40% (800) are returned at $35 refund plus $5 handling, costing $32,000. Safety testing before sale would have cost about $6,000, so the recall costs over five times as much, before reputation damage.
caption: Testing first would have cost about $6,000; the recall costs $32,000.

alt: A four-step analysis chain using Juniper Cafés: the minimum wage rises, the business must pay more for 35,000 hours, this costs $21,000 a year but may motivate staff, so profit falls unless prices rise about 14 cents. The judgement depends on how many staff are affected, rivals’ costs and customers’ reaction to prices.
caption: Law, what the business must do, cost or benefit, effect: then judge.
